lines.text: Then stop reading and start bagging - here's the protocol. Double-bag it in zipper bags and wash your hands; that's not theater, that's keeping the surface clean for whoever analyzes it. Don't polish it, don't cut it, don't put acid on it - every home test destroys something the lab needed. The radiation question gets answered with a thirty-dollar Geiger counter from any hardware site, and I'll save you the suspense: in seventy years of this subject, the pieces that made people sick all turned out to be something else entirely, or nothing at all. Then: GPS the exact spot you found it, note the date and hour, photograph the field before anything else touches it. Heavy, shiny inside, warm at dawn - that could be a hundred years of farm slag, and it could be something else. A field investigator will tell you which in one visit, and he'll bring the tools you shouldn't own.

lines.text: Cease online research; begin handling protocol. Double-bag in zipper polyethylene, then hand hygiene - contamination control for subsequent analysis, not theater. Prohibitions: no polishing, cutting, or acid testing - home methods destroy analytically significant surfaces. Radiation assessment: an inexpensive Geiger counter resolves it empirically; the seventy-year archive contains no verified radiologically hazardous recovered material. Documentation: GPS coordinates of recovery point, date and hour, photographic survey of the field pre-disturbance. Physical characteristics - density, fracture luster, residual warmth - are consistent with century-old slag OR with unclassified material. A field investigator resolves the classification in one visit, with proper instrumentation.
